zuspark

Spark Connect lets a client run Spark SQL on a remote cluster over gRPC. Until now, reaching it from R meant a local Spark installation and its JVM, or a Python environment in between.

zuspark is a Spark Connect client written in R. It connects to an sc:// endpoint, runs SQL there and brings the result back as Arrow or as a data frame, with no JVM, no Python and no Spark installation on your machine.

  • Only R packages. gRPC, protocol buffers and Arrow come from zugrpc, zuproto and zuarrow; zuspark itself has no compiled code.
  • Spark’s own protocol. The message definitions ship with the package, pinned to Spark 4.2.1, and the connection string is PySpark’s.
  • Exact by default. A value R cannot hold exactly is an error, not a silent rounding; you choose its text or a widened type instead.
  • Results that survive a cut. Long results are read with reattachable execution: a stream cut by a proxy or a timeout resumes where it stopped, and the server’s buffer is released as the rows are read.
  • dplyr on Spark. With DBI and dbplyr installed, a session is a DBI connection: tbl() and dplyr verbs become Spark SQL, run on the cluster, and only collect() brings rows back.
  • Databricks too. spark_connect_databricks() connects to a workspace’s serverless compute or to a cluster.

Installation

zuspark is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub; pak also installs its dependencies, which are on GitHub too:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zuspark")

Usage 

library(zuspark)

Connect to a Spark Connect server. A local one listens on port 15002; spark_connect() with no argument reads the SPARK_REMOTE environment variable.

con <- spark_connect("sc://localhost:15002")
spark_version(con)
#> [1] "4.2.1"

spark_sql() sends a query and returns it unexecuted; spark_collect() runs it and returns a data frame.

q <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT id, id % 3 AS bucket, CAST(id AS STRING) AS label FROM range(6)")
spark_collect(q)
#>   id bucket label
#> 1  0      0     0
#> 2  1      1     1
#> 3  2      2     2
#> 4  3      0     3
#> 5  4      1     4
#> 6  5      2     5

The work happens on the server: here Spark aggregates ten million rows, and only seven come back.

spark_collect(spark_sql(con, "
  SELECT id % 7 AS weekday, count(*) AS n
  FROM range(10000000)
  GROUP BY weekday
  ORDER BY weekday
"))
#>   weekday       n
#> 1       0 1428572
#> 2       1 1428572
#> 3       2 1428572
#> 4       3 1428571
#> 5       4 1428571
#> 6       5 1428571
#> 7       6 1428571

Spark’s errors keep Spark’s error class and SQLSTATE.

err <- tryCatch(spark_sql(con, "SELECT * FROM sales"), error = identity)
err$error_class
#> [1] "TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND"
err$sql_state
#> [1] "42P01"
spark_disconnect(con)

With DBI and dbplyr, the same session works with dplyr. The pipeline below is translated to one Spark SQL query by dbplyr’s own Spark backend; Spark summarises a million rows and sends back seven.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
db <- DBI::dbConnect(spark_driver(), "sc://localhost:15002")
trips <- tbl(db, sql("SELECT id % 7 AS weekday, rand(1) * 30 AS minutes FROM range(1000000)"))
trips |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  summarise(trips = n(), minutes = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(weekday) |>
  collect()
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   weekday  trips minutes
#>     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1       0 142858    15.0
#> 2       1 142857    15.0
#> 3       2 142857    15.0
#> 4       3 142857    15.0
#> 5       4 142857    15.0
#> 6       5 142857    15.0
#> 7       6 142857    15.0
DBI::dbDisconnect(db)

Every function but zuspark_info() starts with spark_, and every one after spark_connect() takes the connection, a query or an error first.

Related work

zuspark speaks the protocol defined by Apache Spark’s Spark Connect .proto files, and checks its results against PySpark’s. In R, sparklyr reaches Spark Connect through pysparklyr and Python, and SparkR through a local Spark; spark-connect-go and spark-connect-rust are native clients in other languages.
